prize_parts.citation: for their analysis of how special-interest politics shapes trade policy, and for linking trade to innovation and growth

statement.case_for: Grossman and Helpman turned trade protection from an exogenous policy variable into the equilibrium outcome of lobbying and political competition, in a model that is tractable and delivers testable predictions. That framework still organises theory and applied work on tariffs, trade agreements and political economy. The same pair's joint work on innovation, growth and trade extends the reach beyond trade. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: a decades-long, tightly coupled partnership with joint papers and a joint book, which fits a two-name award without arbitrary exclusions. The core results are about thirty years old and have been tested, extended and absorbed into teaching and policy analysis, so maturity is not a concern. I apply the same criteria to every field. By those criteria the combination of conceptual generality, clean credit and long confirmation is what separates this entry from candidates with diffuse attribution or shorter track records.
statement.case_against: Empirical support for the specific protection-for-sale predictions is mixed, and estimated structural parameters are sensitive to specification, so part of the contribution is an organising framework rather than a settled empirical result. There is also a real question whether the committee sees this as distinct enough from the earlier trade prize (2008) and from the recent recognition of innovation-driven growth. If the committee wanted to reward trade through firm heterogeneity instead, the credited set would change.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the structural IO entry (B002: BLP demand estimation and dynamic industry models) first. He places Grossman-Helpman second and notes that B002 is partly a method, which the committee might weigh against awards tied to a substantive discovery. He also flags that Helpman's presence on another ballot raises a credit question.
responses.response: I agree B002 is very strong. It is a rare case where a method changed policy practice in merger review and antitrust, and I ranked it second. Where I differ is on attribution. The three-name cap forces the BLP triple and leaves out Bresnahan's and Reiss's foundational empirical-IO work, and it splits Pakes's separate dynamic-games contribution from the demand framework. B001 needs no such cut. On Helpman, I read his role in B001 and in B030 as two distinct achievements. The first is the political-economy and growth work with Grossman, and the second is firm heterogeneity with Melitz. Crediting him for the first does not depend on the second, so I do not see a credit problem. I would keep B002 as the leading alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B018 (technology, tasks and the China shock) first, citing credible designs paired with an explanatory framework, a large follow-on literature and strong policy influence. She also lists the identification and persistence debates and the missing task-model antecedents as uncertainties.
responses.response: I accept the empirical quality and the policy relevance, and I ranked neither it nor its designs below the standard I apply to B001. My reservation is about how cleanly it can be credited, not its merit. Her own opening shows the problem: she lists Autor, Hanson and Katz, while others propose Autor, Dorn and Hanson, so the set is not stable. The task framework also has antecedents (Levy and Murnane) and a related line of work already touched by the 2024 prize, and the shift-share and persistence debates are still live. Those issues fall on the very points where a prize citation has to be precise. If the committee can settle a three-name set and a single stated discovery for B018, I would reconsider its standing. Today I find B001 easier to defend on attribution and on how much time has passed.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B001 first on the grounds that the protection-for-sale model gave trade policy a rigorous political-economy foundation. He argues the pair's partnership is the cleanest credit and that adding anyone would dilute it. He also notes the empirical support is mixed and that the committee might prefer to reward trade through the firm-heterogeneity line instead.
responses.response: I agree on the two-name credit, and I share his caution about empirical support. I would not claim the specific functional forms are well confirmed. The contribution is the framework, which produced testable implications and a large body of empirical work, and that is the standard I apply to theory in other fields too. On the firm-heterogeneity alternative, I rank B030 below B001. Melitz's central paper is influential, but Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum established the exporter facts and related models independently, and they are not credited on that ballot. That gap makes B030 harder to attribute than B001. I would not combine the two parts, because the Helpman overlap would then force a three-person configuration and blur the citations.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee places on mixed empirical support for the protection-for-sale predictions versus the framework's influence on research design and policy analysis.
Whether the committee views the contribution as sufficiently distinct from the 2008 trade prize and from the recent recognition of innovation-driven growth.
Whether the citation should centre on political economy of trade policy or also on trade, innovation and growth, since the ballot's stated discovery emphasises the former.
Whether a more diffusely credited but arguably broader candidate, such as B002 or B018, would survive scrutiny better once attribution sets are settled.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in corporate finance (venture capital, private equity, bankruptcy and carbon pricing), and my listed co-authors and institutions do not include any credited name on B001. I note that I am an adjunct at Chicago Booth and have long overlapped with several colleagues on the committee, but I do not treat either as a candidate-specific conflict.
